prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and of its active form, which established the incretin principle underlying treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: I keep a single prize part on B025 with Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The achievement is mature and the evidence is settled: proglucagon processing, the incretin effect, glucose-dependent insulin secretion and satiety were worked out as physiology, and large independent outcome trials and more than a decade of clinical use confirm that the resulting drug class works. The round-1 exchange did not move me on the framing. The chair asks whether Knudsen's work is a discovery in its own right. I accept that half-life extension through albumin binding was a real insight, but it is an insight about how to make a known peptide usable, and the physiology it depends on was already established. A citation that names the hormone's biology and its active form rewards what was found. Mojsov is the one name tied to the identification of the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide, so she belongs in a physiology prize.
statement.case_against: The weakest point is still the third seat. Habener is not among the credited names, Mojsov's priority is described as disputed, and I cannot resolve that dispute from the supplied credit. If the committee reads the prize as discovery plus development, my trio omits the person whose drugs reached patients and the citation will look incomplete. A single-part prize also leaves out CAR-T, which has a direct clinical record. I do not think a second part is justified now. B047 has an unresolved question over Rosenberg and Eshhar, and B009 is conceptually strong but has no approved STING-directed drug. A second part added to satisfy breadth, rather than because it is ready, would weaken the prize.

responses.point: The chair holds that Knudsen's long-acting analogue work was itself a biochemical insight about half-life and albumin binding, and that a prize limited to physiology omits the step that made the hormone usable.
responses.response: I take this seriously and have moved part of the way. I now call it a real mechanistic contribution rather than only an industrial one. It still builds on the DPP-4 and clearance biology of Drucker and Holst, and it is the part of the story where the attribution is least tied to one person, because the work was done by a company team. I would not block a Drucker, Holst and Knudsen trio if the committee finds Mojsov's claim cannot be checked. I would first test that claim against the priority record. I agree that for CAR-T the engineered receptor is the core, which favours a June and Sadelain pair.

responses.point: Perlmann argues that a prize limited to hormone biology omits the step that made it matter, and also says that if the committee wants physiology only, the Mojsov trio is more defensible.
responses.response: We agree on the condition. Your own statement says the Mojsov trio is the right one under a physiology framing, and that is the framing I defend. The disagreement is about whether the committee should reward the discovery or its reduction to practice. I do not think you and I can settle the Mojsov question by preference. It needs the priority evidence on who first showed the insulinotropic activity of the truncated GLP-1(7-36) peptide, and a vote on the Knudsen trio before that evidence is weighed would let the third seat go to whoever has the easier story.

responses.point: Sandberg frames B025 as a physiology-anchored prize that fits the tradition of rewarding discoveries over products, and warns that a single-achievement prize leaves out CAR-T and optogenetics.
responses.response: I agree on the framing and on the tradition. On the second point I differ in degree. Leaving out strong candidates is the cost of a three-person limit and does not justify a second part by itself. I have changed my alternatives. B047 moves ahead of B038 as the second choice, because Sandberg and the chair are right that CAR-T has the more direct medical consequence, while optogenetics is more clearly a tool. I keep B009 as the other alternative for its mechanistic clarity, and I accept that its translation is still unproven.

responses.point: El-Manira answers the chair's question on optogenetics as a discovery in physiology, and keeps the prize on physiology of GLP-1 rather than product development, with B038 and B051 as alternatives.
responses.response: I agree with El-Manira that the citation should reward physiology and the active peptide, and I share the view that the Mojsov seat is defensible but not uniquely correct. On optogenetics I see the case that channelrhodopsin work opened questions in neuroscience, but with six credited names and three seats, any trio omits someone with a real claim. That attribution problem is larger than the one in B025, so I would not add it as a second part this year. B051 is a strong mechanism, but I have not seen it argued as ahead of CAR-T on medical consequence.

uncertainties: Whether the priority evidence supports Mojsov or Habener for the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide, and whether Habener's absence from the credited names is a real gap.
Whether the committee frames B025 as physiology or as physiology plus development, since this decides the third seat.
Whether a second part would be stronger than none, given the unresolved credit questions for B047 (Rosenberg, Eshhar) and the attribution spread for B038.
Whether the clinical record for cGAS-STING will mature, which bears on its rank in later years.
statement.conflict_note: No change to my disclosure. I co-authored the 2016 spatial transcriptomics paper and have documented co-authorships with Rickard Sandberg and others, but none of the credited names on B025 or the alternatives B047 and B009 are among them, so I see no recusal issue.
